title: Acceleration data-based robust on-board monitoring of hunting proximity in railway vehicles under uncertainty: A feasibility study
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the International Conference on Noise and Vibration Engineering (ISMA 2026), Leuven, Belgium, 2026
summary: The feasibility of on-board, real-time proximity assessment to railway hunting initiation under uncertainty arising from vehicle/track and other operational conditions is assessed. In this context, a novel method that classifies hunting proximity into one of several prespecified speed proximity intervals is introduced, based on a grey nonlinear vehicle model with parameters estimated from on-board acceleration measurements and model-based estimation of the Maximum Lyapunov Exponent (MLE) as a hunting proximity measure. The method's performance and robustness are assessed via Monte Carlo simulations using a MATLAB-based multi-body vehicle model and four operating scenarios. The method is shown to achieve excellent performance achieving 97.08 % classification accuracy, which marks a significant improvement over a potential alternative. Its robustness to faulty suspensions and hollow-worn wheels is also demonstrated, although certain performance compromise is observed under worn-track conditions.

title: Multichannel Sampling and Reconstruction in Multidimensional Shift-Invariant Spaces
summary: We develop a multichannel sampling and reconstruction framework for multidimensional principal shift-invariant spaces based on a finite-dimensional polyphase representation. Periodic nonuniform shifts and derivative measurements are modeled as analysis channels, leading to a frequency-domain linear system relating the measurements to the polyphase components of the underlying coefficient sequence. Stable recovery is characterized through uniform singular-value bounds on the associated polyphase matrix, and explicit synthesis kernels are obtained from its Moore Penrose left inverse. The formulation applies to both separable and genuinely non-separable generators and includes several classical one dimensional sampling formulas as special cases. For irregular derivative measurements, where the periodic polyphase structure is no longer directly available, we develop an iterative reconstruction method based on local bivariate Hermite interpolation followed by orthogonal projection onto the shift-invariant space. A sufficient contraction condition is derived to guarantee geometric convergence of the iteration. Numerical experiments demonstrate the reconstruction performance for separable and non-separable generators and illustrate robustness to additive measurement noise and sampling-location perturbations.

title: MtReNIRS: A Self-Supervised Foundation Model for Transferable Neurovascular Representations
summary: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) offers a promising approach for monitoring the hemodynamic correlates of neural activity in naturalistic settings. However, existing modeling methods for fNIRS are largely confined to small-scale, single-session data with low sampling rates, driven by high heterogeneity in acquisition devices and optode montages. In addition, the complex spatiotemporal structure of fNIRS signals further restricts model scalability and transferability across settings. As a result, it remains unclear whether a single fNIRS encoder can learn representations that are usable across subjects, tasks, devices, and montages. Here, we show that a montage-aware masked autoencoder, pretrained on 12 public fNIRS datasets spanning 268 subjects and 567 recording hours, learns generalizable neurovascular representations that transfer across three external datasets. Our fNIRS foundation model, MtReNIRS, jointly encodes the slow hemodynamic nature of fNIRS, chromophore identity and cortical location by mapping heterogeneous montages onto a shared anatomical reference. MtReNIRS achieves cross-subject performance on par or better than fully supervised baselines and excels in few-shot within-subject calibration, where it outperforms prior state-of-the-art fNIRS models, while remaining robust to sparse montages. Our results indicate that montage-aware self-supervision yields physiologically grounded, transferable fNIRS representations, providing a scalable foundation for label-efficient brain-computer interfaces.

title: Neural fields for adaptive white matter microstructural modeling
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures. Accepted to SPIE Medical Imaging 2027: Image Processing
summary: Diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is sensitive to the micron-level diffusion motion of water molecules, allowing in vivo characterization of white matter architecture in the brain. Microstructural models like diffusion tensors or the Standard Model are typically fit independently on each voxel, limiting their ability to incorporate local spatial context and adapt to regional tissue complexity. Here, we introduce FiberField, an approach using neural fields that selects from multiple candidate models with different numbers of fibers to estimate fiber configurations and properties. This method incorporates spatial context through coordinate representations and model-weighted priors inspired by Bayesian model averaging to adapt to local microstructure. To compare FiberField with ground truth fiber properties, we validate on simulated diffusion MRI before applying to in vivo data. In simulated diffusion MRI, FiberField accurately estimates fiber directions and diffusivities using a multi-stick model (angular error: $2.2 \pm 2.8°$, diffusivity root mean square error (RMSE): $4.4 \times 10^{-4} \pm 5.2 \times 10^{-4}$ mm$^{2}$/s, fiber sensitivity: $0.87 \pm 0.21$). FiberField resolves fibers at 25% smaller angular separations than fod2fixel, and the diffusivity RMSE is 52% lower within fiber crossings than the Standard Model. On acquired diffusion MRI, FiberField's estimated fiber directions agree with those from MRtrix3's fod2fixel while also mapping microstructural properties such as diffusivity (angular difference: $10.5 \pm 7.1°$). Using neural fields allows for adaptive white matter modeling for selecting from a set of alternative models while maintaining accurate fiber property estimation.

title: Causal sensitivity analyses for indirect and spillover mediation effects in cluster-randomized trials: Application to a pragmatic trial on chronic pain management
summary: Causal mediation in cluster-randomized trials can clarify whether a cluster-level intervention changes patient outcomes through patient- and peer-level processes, but identification relies on untestable cross-world assumptions. We develop a two-part sensitivity analysis for violations of two distinct cross-world independence assumptions. The first component adapts bridge score sensitivity analysis to assess residual mediator-outcome confounding with clustered mediator exposures; the second uses a Gaussian copula to assess cross-world dependence between an individual's treated mediator and summaries of control-arm peer mediators. The resulting framework parameterizes unidentifiable dependence structures using interpretable correlation parameters and combines them with a flexible Bayesian nonparametric model to characterize the plausible range of the target estimands. A nested common-atoms enriched Dirichlet process models the observed data and supports posterior-predictive standardization. We apply the framework to the Pain Program for Active Coping and Training trial, a primary care-embedded cognitive behavioral therapy intervention for adults with chronic pain receiving long-term opioid therapy. The intervention had a negative total effect on twelve-month pain-related disability. The natural indirect and direct effect decomposition was sensitive to plausible directional residual confounding, whereas the spillover and individual mediation effect decomposition changed little across the copula sensitivity analyses and attributed most of the negative indirect signal to the individual's mediator. Jointly relaxing both assumptions substantially increased uncertainty about the pathways. The analysis supports an overall improvement in disability and a plausible individual pain-impact pathway, while showing that detailed mechanistic claims remain assumption-dependent.

title: KORA: Deterministic-First Execution Control for AI Workloads
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Code and benchmark available at https://github.com/Krako-Labs/KORA
summary: AI applications often invoke a model before they determine whether inference is necessary. That default is useful for ambiguous generative tasks, but it is poorly matched to work that is structured, deterministic, policy-bound, lookup-oriented, or directly verifiable. KORA introduces deterministic-first execution control: a pre-inference control layer that represents requests as task paths, attempts deterministic or structured routes first, validates route outcomes, records telemetry, and escalates to a model-candidate path only when deterministic handling is insufficient. This paper presents KORA as a deterministic-first execution-control architecture and reports bounded evidence from reproducible benchmark and validation workloads. In a reproducible 100-task deterministic-heavy benchmark, KORA-controlled execution avoided 80 of 100 simulated model invocations versus a naive direct baseline, with zero mismatches in the deterministic subset. The workload is intentionally deterministic-heavy: it includes categories such as FAQ lookup, policy/rule checking, schema or format validation, deterministic transformation, and a smaller set of model-needed ambiguous or generative tasks. A separate synthetic customer-support local/no-network validation workload demonstrates route measurement and avoided model-call accounting in an application-shaped setting. These results support bounded model-invocation reduction and validation visibility in documented workloads. They do not establish production behavior, real-provider outcomes, energy outcomes, API-cost reduction, or broad superiority.

title: Improving Learned AC-OPF Feasibility under Distribution Shift with PF-in-the-Loop Correction
summary: Learning-based AC-OPF enables fast dispatch, yet its feasibility can degrade under distribution shift. We analyze three state-of-the-art methods and identify a shared deployment-time limitation: none use feedback from the power-flow (PF)-realized state to ensure feasibility of the predicted control. Using a simple PF-in-the-loop feasibility restoration filter, we empirically show that such feedback substantially improves hard feasibility across four out-of-distribution scenarios with modest runtime overhead.

title: Quantile Regression Postprocessing with Negative Electricity Price Forecasts
summary: Negative electricity prices create market-relevant risks for trading, bidding, renewable revenues, and flexibility valuation. Quantile regression-based postprocessing is a widely used approach for converting point forecasts into predictive distributions. We show that the standard specification, which imposes a single linear relationship between the point forecast and predictive quantiles, can become structurally incoherent when the conditioning point forecast is negative. In such cases, the resulting predictive distribution may exhibit not only ordinary quantile crossing, where adjacent quantiles are in the wrong order, but also a severe version of crossing, which we refer to as tail-quantile inversion. This can reverse downside and upside risk signals. To address this problem, we propose sign-dependent QR-based postprocessing specifications that allow the quantile function to differ between positive and negative point forecasts. Using German day-ahead electricity prices as an empirical illustration, we show that these specifications improve predictive accuracy, particularly for negative point forecasts and for extreme probability levels. Moreover, when combined with joint estimation across quantiles, the sign-dependent specifications largely eliminate tail-quantile inversion and all quantile crossing. The results demonstrate that the sign of the point forecast should be explicitly accounted for when constructing probabilistic forecasts in markets where negative prices can occur.

title: Packet Interval Modulation-based NFC for Scalable IoT around Meandered E-textile
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to IEEE Globecom 2026
summary: Near-field communication (NFC) sensor tags are promising for low-cost, scalable environmental monitoring due to their battery-free, maintenance-free operation. Recent advances in NFC reader garments, integrated with conductive textile coils, allow users to interact seamlessly with tags scattered across their daily environment. However, dynamically identifying and reading out a fluctuating number of tags remains challenging. If multiple tags speak and collide, they must randomly retry until an empty slot is found. Standard NFC identifies tags using time-slotted ALOHA, which assigns tags to fixed time slots. If multiple tags speak and collide, they must retry with a tag filter to avoid collision until all tags are identified. This rigid setup is fragile in dynamic settings; as tags enter and leave the communication range, the heavy overhead of slot re-negotiation and inevitable collisions restricts data throughput. Here, we propose an asynchronous NFC based on packet interval modulation. By treating minimal ID-only packets as pulses and encoding data in their intervals, we enable communication through silence. This ensures the channel remains mostly unoccupied, drastically reducing collisions even in high-density environments. Our simulations show that for ten tags, our method achieves a 4-fold increase in throughput compared to the ALOHA approach. Furthermore, the system remains robust, maintaining over 160 bps/tag throughput even under extreme fluctuations in the number of tags over 20.

title: Distribution Grid Reconfiguration and Restoration via Linearizable Multi-phase Power Flow Modeling
summary: Accurate and tractable power-flow (PF) modeling is essential for distribution grid topology optimization, where the presence of discrete branch-status decisions therein significantly increase the computational complexity. To tackle this challenge, we develop a topology-adaptive, low-complexity neural piecewise-linear (N-PWL) PF model. We propose a sequential layer design that can directly incorporate branch status variables into the PF mapping from branch flows to nodal injections. As a result, our N-PWL model not only preserves the PF branch-node consistency but also facilitates the representation of any unseen topologies without retraining. A low-complexity model design is further pursued to attain a linear NN parameter scaling by using a fixed-size area partition of the feeder. The resulting scalable N-PWL model enables mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulations of feeder topology optimization tasks, including distribution network reconfiguration (DNR) and restoration ordering problems (ROP). Numerical studies on the unbalanced, multi-phase IEEE 123-bus feeder demonstrate our N-PWL model outperforms existing end-to-end baselines in PF prediction and, more importantly, can fill the gap by achieving accurate representation of any unseen topologies. For solving DNR/ROP, our model can significantly improve the AC feasibility over linearized PF models, with a notable reduction of computation time compared with AC-PF based nonlinear formulations, particularly under a large number of topology decisions.

title: Evaluating the Predictive Validity of ICT's Accumulation-Manipulation-Distribution (AMD) Model on CME E-Mini NASDAQ-100 Futures
summary: To our knowledge, this paper provides the first systematic quantitative evaluation of the ICT Accumulation-Manipulation-Distribution (AMD) model on CME E-Mini NASDAQ-100 futures (NQ). The AMD model proposes that institutional participants structure intraday price delivery in three phases: overnight accumulation in the Asian session, a deliberate false breakout during London, and directional delivery to the opposing liquidity pool during the New York morning session. Using four years of real 15-minute OHLCV data from Databento (January 2022 to July 2026), we operationalize the AMD rules into a strict mechanical strategy and analyze the statistical properties of the resulting signal across N = 484 manipulation signal days using chi-square testing, Benjamini-Hochberg multiple comparisons correction, and regime-conditional analysis. Three principal findings emerge. First, the AMD manipulation signal fires on 44% of trading days. Second, 57% of valid signals see full target delivery before the 9:40 AM New York entry window opens, revealing a structural mismatch between the model's timing assumptions and actual price delivery. Third, within this operationalization of the AMD model, no directional information beyond the daily trend regime was observed: when the signal aligns with the trend it is correct 62-71% of the time (Cohen's h = 0.23-0.43); when it opposes the trend it is correct only 25-30% of the time (Cohen's h = 0.42-0.53). All four trending-regime cells survive Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Key findings are robust to variation in the manipulation breach threshold (5-20 NQ points), Asia range filter percentile, and stop buffer. The regime-dependent signal pattern constitutes a specific, testable hypothesis for follow-on research.

title: Real-Time Smart Retail Analytics through Fog Computing using the RetailLightNet Lightweight Model
comment: 2025 5th International Conference on Mobile Networks and Wireless Communications (ICMNWC), Conference Location: Tumkur, India
summary: Smart retail systems now depend on the application of real-time video analytics, which can track customer behavior, manage shelf inventory, and enhance in-store processes. Currently cloud-based applications of video analytics face multiple challenges such as high latency of the communication itself, privacy concerns surrounding transmitting raw video, and the computational demands of the heavy vision models used on the often limited network infrastructure. These challenges lead to delays in decision making where prompt action is crucial. To address these short comings, this research proposes Fog-based analytics withRetailLightNet (F RLN), an ultra lightweight deep learning model which is specifically suited for the edge, resource constrained hardware capabilities of devices like the NVIDIA Jetson Nano. The approach utilizes publicly available retail datasets, SKU110K, and RPC, which contains an assortment of product, shelf, and customer interaction scenarios for training.The processes include preprocessing images through normalization and employing motion-gated frame selection to improve efficiency by omitting redundant frames to ease the workload on the fog processing. Internal within Retail LightNet, image feature extraction is realized through depth wise separable convolutions which help support spatial and channel-wise learning without heavy computational costs. The model employs two prediction heads presence classification, and density regression, supporting shelf monitoring and queue assessment. The proposed F RLN framework attained better results in terms of precision (0.988), recall (0.976), and F1-score(0.976) when compared with existing convolutional neural network. Keywords: fog computing, motion-gated frame selection,NVIDIA jetson, retail lightnet, smart retail.

title: Multi-time-scale Control of Power Systems
summary: The power grid has been dominated by large synchronous generators and clearly separated control layers. Today, power-electronics energy conversion interfaces are rapidly being deployed calling for another look at system-level control hierarchies. This article examines how multi-time-scale modeling, feedback control, and feedback optimization can help reinterpret the traditional organically grown hierarchy of primary control, automatic generation control, and economic dispatch, and enable new approaches for control of contemporary power systems. Beginning with an overview of power system models and conventional operational practices, the article develops connections to modern control architectures that can coordinate heterogeneous resources, account for operational constraints, and exploit faster actuation without overlooking first-principles physics.

title: Manipulation-Resistant Oracles via Continuous Peer Prediction
comment: 27 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at MARBLE 2026, Limassol, Cyprus, 16-18 September 2026
summary: Blockchain oracle networks, including decentralised physical infrastructure networks (DePINs), report physical measurements from a source that can manipulate the underlying process. A carbon project operator, for example, can dry a site before measurement and be paid for soil organic carbon (SOC) that was never stored. Peer prediction covers discrete signals under a strategic source, or continuous reports under an honest source, but not both at once. We close that gap for Gaussian reports. Strict propriety of the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) settles the reporting stage alone. Our result concerns the source stage. A report-only settlement rule whose honest-source payoff is non-decreasing in the true value identifies and deters source manipulation if and only if the sensors respond to that manipulation by different amounts. When they respond identically, manipulation is observationally equivalent to a genuine rise in SOC, and CRPS translation equivariance leaves every peer score unchanged, so no such rule deters the source. Necessity follows from invariance rather than from the signal enumeration available in the discrete case. The source-stage estimator is ordinary weighted least squares, and the contribution is the characterisation around it. With eight calibrated SOC models on 37,280 real European soil spectra, shift-naive aggregators over-credit by up to 57% under a calibrated moisture perturbation while the joint estimate stays near-unbiased. The guarantee holds on the equilibrium path for non-colluding reporters and inherits the models' own calibration error. The project page is at https://rqcker.github.io/crps-wls.

title: NSB2: An Open-Source Modular Pipeline for Application-Network Co-Simulation
comment: Submitted to ACM Middleware 2026 for publication
summary: As connected applications -- from intelligence-enabled assistants and the smart homes to autonomous vehicles and large-scale Internet-of-Things deployments -- become increasingly pervasive, their performance, safety, and reliability depend more than ever on the underlying network. Designing and validating such systems therefore requires development environments that holistically account for both application and network behavior. While network simulators and emulators provide high-fidelity models of network behavior, connecting full-fledged applications to them remains difficult due to platform constraints, simulator-specific interfaces, and narrow single-purpose integrations. To address this gap, we present NSB2 (Network Simulation Bridge 2), an open-source network co-simulation middleware that relays payloads between application processes through a network simulator. NSB2 is composed of a central daemon and thin, embedded application- and simulator-side libraries for flexible integration, disentangled communication channels for unencumbered inter-process communications, and in-memory key-value storage for efficient payload caching and retrieval. NSB2 is designed to be lightweight, accessible, and extensible: it exposes streamlined interfaces supported in Python and C++, modular internal abstractions that let users swap or extend network simulation/emulation backends, flexible and configurable deployment modes, and integration helpers for the widely-used ns-3 and OMNeT++ network simulators. Our evaluation across multiple co-simulation scenarios shows that NSB2 introduces negligible memory and latency overhead, enabling researchers and developers to achieve richer, more realistic modeling of connected systems with minimum overhead.

title: When Slides Met Scans: Cross-Attention for Renal Cancer Prognosis
summary: Histopathology and computed tomography (CT) provide complementary views of renal cancer. We connect these modalities through bidirectional cross-attention between 16 histology prototypes and up to 32 kidney-centered CT tokens from frozen foundation models. In 210 TCGA-KIRC patients with 46 disease-specific survival (DSS) events, 5-fold evaluation yielded a C-index of $0.760\pm0.081$ and 3-year AUROC of 0.773 (95\% CI 0.678--0.860), the highest averages among evaluated unimodal and fusion baselines. External testing in 180 CPTAC-CCRCC patients yielded DSS C-index of 0.629 with CT withheld. Attribution analysis linked predictions to image regions while exposing acquisition artifacts. These findings support further study of cross-scale fusion and independent multimodal validation.

title: CircaFMM: A Flexible Statistical Framework for Circadian Rhythmicity Detection in Transcriptomics
comment: Supplementary Data 1 and 2 are available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request
summary: Detecting circadian rhythmicity in large-scale transcriptomic data is challenging when sampling is irregular, signals are weak, and expression profiles deviate from sinusoidal shapes. The fixed harmonic form of classical Cosinor-based methods may therefore be poorly suited to asymmetric and temporally complex rhythms. We present CircaFMM, a flexible framework for circadian rhythmicity detection based on the single-component Frequency Modulated Möbius (FMM) model. CircaFMM defines rhythmicity as time dependence induced by the Möbius phase parameter, so that the non-rhythmic null corresponds to a time-invariant mean profile. The resulting non-regular test combines time-density weighting, regularized estimation, and bootstrap calibration of a weighted likelihood-ratio-type statistic. Simulations showed controlled type-I error under irregular sampling and improved power over the classical Cosinor F-test for asymmetric waveforms. Applied to the GTEx-13T postmortem transcriptomic dataset, CircaFMM recovered canonical clock genes and circadian pathways while identifying additional rhythmic candidates with lower signal-to-noise-ratio, greater waveform asymmetry, and non-sinusoidal temporal profiles. CircaFMM is available at https://circafmm.shinyapps.io/circafmm_shinyapp/, with source code at https://github.com/FMMGroupVa/CircaFMM.

title: IoT-based Smart Real-Time Energy-Aware Server Room Monitoring System
summary: The integration of the Internet of Things (IoT) into monitoring systems has become increasingly significant across various fields, including energy management, environmental monitoring, and industrial applications. This paper proposes a smart, real-time, energy-aware monitoring system architecture for IoT using a brokerless Data Distribution Service (DDS) middleware. Environmental and electrical metrics are transmitted with high reliability, achieving an average latency of 1.76 milliseconds and a throughput of 57.1 Mbps. These metrics are processed by a multi-head Long Short-Term Memory network. Evaluated on the empirical TDC2.0 data center dataset, the architecture simultaneously performs three tasks: predicting thermal stress, detecting cooling inefficiency, and forecasting multi-step cooling power demand. The multi task network achieved an F1-score of 0.92 for proactive thermal stress prediction and demonstrated the capability to identify systemic cooling anomalies. Furthermore, the model generated consistent power forecasts across 5-minute, 10-minute, and 30 minute horizons, maintaining an R2 > 0.83. A post-hoc SHAP analysis indicated that the predictive logic aligns with established thermodynamic relationships. Overall, the proposed architecture offers a transparent and low-latency framework for critical facility management.

title: Data-Driven Hamiltonian for Neural Optimal Control
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a prominent data-driven approach to optimal control, but often requires substantial amounts of data and provides limited guarantees when encountering out-of-distribution state-action pairs. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach grounded in the well-established Hamilton-Jacobi framework in optimal control theory. Rather than requiring an explicit analytical model of the system dynamics to evaluate the Hamiltonian, we replace this with a data-driven Hamiltonian (DDH), which we generalize to a broad class of optimal control problems. In contrast to standard RL approaches, the DDH provides a principled mechanism, requiring only minimal prior system information such as a Lipschitz constant, for quantifying and accounting for uncertainty in regions not covered by the data, enabling the derivation of controllers with performance guarantees. Additional prior system knowledge, when available, can be readily incorporated to improve performance. For high-dimensional systems, we further introduce a physics-informed neural approximation of the value function, trained using a novel procedure that generates worst-case fictitious rollouts evaluated through the DDH. On an LQR problem, the DDH reaches near-optimal cost on every dataset we test, including random data on which offline RL methods remain far from optimal, and needs far fewer samples than online RL. On a nonlinear lunar lander benchmark, the DDH achieves an optimality gap to a trajectory-optimization reference more than $3\times$ smaller than CQL and FQL, and matches the performance of SAC with approximately $37\times$ fewer samples. These results establish the DDH as a promising framework for data-driven optimal control, particularly in settings where available data are limited in quantity or quality.

title: Reconstructing the Human Development Index at the Individual Level from Survey Microdata: Development and Validation of a Methodology
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures. Replication notebook and data archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22714205
summary: This study proposes and validates a methodology for reconstructing the Human Development Index (HDI) from individual-level survey microdata, enabling disaggregated estimates for demographic subpopulations while maintaining coherence with the official HDI. Data from 40,185 respondents in 21 countries from the European Social Survey (ESS7, 2014) were analysed, combined with World Bank indicators for life expectancy, gross national income per capita, and expected years of schooling. The health dimension was estimated from national life expectancy, adjusted by self-rated health; income, by a lognormal multiplier calibrated by the Gini coefficient; and education, by combining observed and expected years of schooling. The dimensions were aggregated by geometric mean, weighted by sampling weights, with confidence intervals estimated via the delta method. Among the 39,706 individuals with valid data (98.8%), the reconstructed HDI showed high agreement with the official 2014 HDI, with a mean absolute error of 0.0099 and a Pearson correlation of 0.917. Consistent differences across subgroups evidenced the methodology's convergent validity and its capacity to produce disaggregated estimates of human development, expanding the HDI's potential for analyses of socioeconomic and demographic inequalities.

title: Where Does My Call Go? Measuring Google Meet, Zoom, and Microsoft Teams on Starlink
comment: accepted to present at the LEONET 2026
summary: Low-Earth-Orbit (LEO) satellite networks are expanding broadband access, but major Real-Time Communication (RTC) platforms, including Google Meet, Zoom, and Microsoft Teams, still rely on service-point selection mechanisms that appear to be largely shaped by terrestrial-network assumptions. As a result, they may not consistently account for LEO-specific dynamics such as satellite topology and Point-of-Presence (PoP) changes, especially during in-flight connectivity. To characterize RTC service-point selection over Starlink, we measure RTC performance using a Canada-wide testbed and more than 24 hours of in-flight experiments. Our results show clear platform differences. Google Meet tends to align more closely with the serving PoP, consistent with broader observed edge coverage. Zoom follows a regional service-point selection pattern, while Microsoft Teams often remains tied to fixed service points. Moreover, we show that in-flight PoP handovers can shift traffic egress points mid-session, and that RTC platforms respond differently to these changes. In some cases, this interaction leads to suboptimal service-point selections and RTT inflation. Overall, our findings suggest that LEO connectivity can expose mismatches between Starlink egress dynamics and RTC service-point selection, motivating further measurement and LEO-optimized designs for service placement and selection.

title: Electric Vehicle Scheduling and Carbon-Aware Energy Dispatch for Charging Stations
summary: Electric vehicle (EV) charging stations integrating photovoltaic (PV) generation, battery storage, and bidirectional grid exchange must coordinate access to limited chargers with energy supply while considering both energy cost and carbon emissions. This paper proposes a solver-free greedy heuristic (SFGH) for dynamic vehicle scheduling (VS) and a twin delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (TD3) controller for carbon-aware energy dispatch (ED). SFGH assigns EVs according to reductions in service delays, and TD3 controls battery operation to balance energy costs and carbon emissions while meeting the resulting charging demand. The model allows both PV and battery exports, accounting for export revenue and carbon credits. Simulations on year-long case studies show that SFGH--TD3 achieves the lowest accumulated service delay, energy cost, and carbon emissions among the evaluated heuristic and multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (DRL) configurations.

title: Bayesian Recovery Trajectories Following Forced Sexual Experience: Healthcare Access and Social Support Among Women
comment: Submitted to Social Psychiatry and Psychiatric Epidemiology
summary:
\textbf{Background.} Women who experience forced sexual violence face elevated risks of poor mental and physical health, but whether long-term health follows distinct trajectories and whether healthcare access and social support differentiate them remains unclear.
  \textbf{Methods.} We analyzed 1,848 women from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health), followed from adolescence into adulthood. An identified Bayesian mixture model classified joint mental and physical health burden trajectories from six repeated indicators. Bayesian logistic models estimated associations of forced sexual experience, healthcare access, social support, and demographics with trajectory membership. Robustness was assessed across three mixture specifications and four- and five-class alternatives.
  \textbf{Results.} We retained three classes: low-burden/resilient (27.2\% posterior mean weight), moderate/worsening burden (43.2\%), and high chronic burden (29.7\%). All specifications converged ($\hat{R}=1.00$) with well-separated classes; four- and five-class alternatives had convergence problems or an unstable additional class. Forced sexual experience was associated with higher posterior odds of high chronic burden (OR = 3.78, 95\% credible interval [CrI] 2.84--5.04) and moderate/worsening burden (OR = 1.63, 95\% CrI 1.26--2.12). Better healthcare access and greater social connectedness were independently associated with lower posterior odds of high chronic burden.
  \noindent\textbf{Conclusions.} Long-term health after forced sexual experience follows heterogeneous trajectories. Healthcare access and social connectedness distinguish more favorable trajectories and represent modifiable targets for trauma-informed, longitudinal, survivor-centered care.

title: Calibrated for Which Policy? Conformal Uncertainty for Fixed World Models Under Intervention
summary: Changing a deployment policy can invalidate a world model's uncertainty while leaving the physical transition mechanism and predictor unchanged. For one-step prediction, if source and target laws share the conditional mechanism $P(Y|X)=Q(Y|X)$, then the intervention is identified by the pre-outcome change of measure $w(X)=dQ_X/dP_X$. For policy-controlled dynamics this ratio factors into state-occupancy and action-propensity terms. Weighted conformal calibration transports marginal coverage to the target law; with an estimated ratio $\hat w$, $P_Q\{Y \in C_{\hat w}(X)\} \ge 1-α-TV(Q,\hat Q) \ge 1-α-E_P|w-\hat w|$. Population log-loss regret for a source-versus-target domain classifier bounds the same ratio error. If $h$ is its clipped target posterior, $ρ$ is the target-domain prior, and $Δ(h)$ is population log-loss regret, then $E_P|w-\hat w_h| \le (1/(ργ))\sqrt{Δ(h)/2}$. An exact cancellation improves the dependence from a generic odds-map bound of order $γ^{-2}$ to $(ργ)^{-1}$. Our experiments use a released DINO-feature world model and physical Franka trajectories. Under the strongest controlled state-action shift, ordinary 90% conformal sets cover 55.0%, whereas oracle and learned-ratio calibration cover 91.0% and 90.9%. The learned surrogate remains within 0.9% total variation of the target law. Calibration is relative to the deployment law: the model can remain fixed while calibration follows the intervention. We machine-check in Lean 4 the finite-support algebraic and causal identities used in the classifier-regret argument, including its coverage-composition step.

title: Phase-Coordinated Model Predictive Control for AI Training Power Smoothing
summary: Periodic power fluctuations from artificial intelligence (AI) training workloads can excite oscillations in power systems. This paper proposes a model predictive control (MPC) framework that exploits short start-time delays to mitigate power fluctuations at the computing source. By coordinating the relative phases of independent training jobs, the proposed method reduces the superposition of oscillatory power components without interrupting running jobs or requiring additional power-smoothing hardware. To obtain a tractable optimization formulation, cosine and sine projections are employed to quantify the dominant oscillatory power components, and their magnitudes are used to construct a convex quadratic power-smoothing objective. The receding-horizon framework updates launch decisions as new workload information becomes available while maintaining scheduling feasibility under limited computation time. Numerical results demonstrate reductions of 74.39\% in mean-square power fluctuations within the 0.2--2-Hz band and 46.6\% in power standard deviation, with an average launch delay of 2.188~s. All launch deadlines are satisfied, and the maximum end-to-end computation time is 0.390~s, below the 0.50-s MPC update period.

title: Beyond Greenwashing: Algorithmic Resilience and the Non-Linear Governance Premium in Sovereign Capital Flows
summary: Despite the proliferation of sovereign Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) metrics, traditional linear macro-financial models systematically misprice Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) tail risks during systemic shocks. This paper demonstrates that sovereign risk transmission is fundamentally non-linear. Using a forward-chained global panel of 147 sovereign entities (2010-2024), we deploy a gradient boosting architecture that compresses forecast errors by over 39% against L1-regularized baselines precisely during extreme macroeconomic tail events. Moving beyond opaque predictive accuracy, we apply dual interpretability frameworks to mathematically map the discrete threshold effects of institutional quality. We identify a strict, non-linear "Governance Premium": incremental environmental and social improvements yield zero capital advantage until a foundational regulatory threshold is breached. Finally, we establish regime-conditional 95% uncertainty bounds that maintain valid marginal coverage even under severe ESG reporting failures. This framework equips policymakers with a distribution-free tool to quantify sovereign tail-risk, proving that global capital markets price institutional resilience as a discrete boundary rather than a continuous premium.

title: StereoSplat: Metric-Scale Novel View Synthesis via Stereo-Grounded Gaussian Splatting
summary: We present StereoSplat, a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting architecture designed explicitly for stereo videos to achieve reliable, metric-scale novel-view synthesis. Unlike monocular approaches that neglect the nature of binocular pairs, StereoSplat adopts a native stereo architecture that extracts dense multi-scale latent features and disparity from a foundation stereo backbone and feeds them into a dedicated Gaussian decoder. Our decoder utilizes cross-view feature fusion and gated depth refinement to directly translate these rich representations into per-pixel 3D Gaussians. To resolve the high redundancy of per-pixel predictions across overlapping views, we propose a learnable depth-adaptive aggregation mechanism that clusters and aggregates primitives in inverse-depth space while preserving fine-grained details. To support training and generalization, we introduce XRStereo, a large-scale synthetic dataset of stereo video featuring various rig configurations tailored to match the physical hardware of real-world platforms. Trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated across challenging benchmarks, StereoSplat yields substantial improvements in the depth accuracy of rendered novel views over established baselines while maintaining high-fidelity novel view synthesis. The model also transfers zero-shot to real-world stereo video, with applications in mixed reality, autonomous driving, and robotics.

title: A Topology-Aware Neural Network for Fault Location With Missing Measurements
summary: This paper proposes a topology-aware neural network-based fault locator (TANFL) for radial distribution feeders, which uses voltage and current phasors obtained after the decay of fault induced transients, as well as feeder connection relationships and line parameters, as inputs. The shared bus encoder, bus readout module, and gated line readout module work together to identify the faulty bus or line and estimate the continuous fault location on the selected line. During training, explicit missing data indicators and random bus data block masking are introduced, enabling a single trained model to handle both complete measurement sets and scenarios where any permitted bus measurement device fails. On the IEEE 15 bus feeder, this paper compares TANFL with a conventional multilayer perceptron (MLP) and the formula-based localization method under identical data, measurement availability scenarios, and evaluation metrics. On the test partition, TANFL outperforms the conventional MLP; with complete measurements, its line fault location performance is slightly lower than that of the formula-based method, but in the average results for scenarios with one missing bus measurement block, its accuracy is the highest among the three methods at a 5% tolerance.

title: A Sphericity Filter for Space-Filling Designs in Nondeterministic Experiments
comment: 30 pages: 20-page main article with 5 figures and 5 numbered tables, followed by a 10-page supplement with 2 figures and 9 numbered tables
summary: Space-filling designs support flexible modeling in noisy multi-response experiments, but an individual design can give poor precision for low-order effects. We use a low-order working model to identify effects whose estimation precision we seek to protect, while allowing a more complex final response model. The filter selects one complete design from a candidate pool by minimizing a geometric loss divided by sphericity, without exchanging or altering its points. Sphericity measures the balance of the working-model confidence ellipsoid's principal-axis variances, independently of its volume. In a working-model basis orthonormal over the prediction region, sphericity is the shape factor of the I-criterion, which measures average prediction variance. In cube studies with quadratic least-squares and Gaussian-process fits, this target filter gives modest average prediction gains over the geometrically best candidate at small geometric cost. Gains in working-model precision are largest near saturation: in a four-factor example, worst-decile prediction standard error falls by about a quarter relative to the geometrically best candidate. In constrained mixtures, raw coefficient-based filtering and A-optimality can emphasize extrapolated Scheffe coefficients and yield poor regional prediction precision. Target filtering improves regional working-model precision in most settings studied, mirroring the advantage of I- over A-optimality for highly constrained mixture designs.

title: ObjectTwin: Measuring the Asset Correspondence Gap for Capture-Anchored Digital Twins
summary: Object-wise reconstruction increasingly inserts generated meshes into captured scenes as editable proxies for observed objects. This use creates a requirement absent from isolated-asset scores and pose estimates: at the captured metric state, the proxy should reproduce calibrated observations of the same instance. We present ObjectTwin, a scan-grounded measurement protocol that freezes the instance, cameras, scan-projected support and recorded depth, metric anchor, and evaluation denominator, then replaces only the object representation. The resulting asset correspondence gap measures lost observation agreement relative to scan-derived visible geometry without treating the scan as complete physical ground truth. Across two indoor RGB-D capture domains and two generation backends, visible, anchored generated assets lose 0.302-0.497 MaskIoU under this replacement. Every tested scene-level estimate is positive, while same-input generator preference reverses across capture domains. Coverage and overlap-depth analyses locate disagreement in both visible support and surface placement; the evaluated conservative pose refinement does not systematically recover it. These results establish capture correspondence as a separately measurable interface between generated-asset quality and stronger physical or task-level evaluation.

title: Thermal-Mass Coupled Modeling and Optimal Scheduling of Aluminum Smelting Loads for Safe Demand Response Participation
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid. DOI: 10.1109/TSG.2026.3736640. This is the author-accepted manuscript
summary: Aluminum smelting loads (ASLs) offer substantial flexibility potential, yet their actual participation in demand response remains conservative owing to the risk of operational failures. Power adjustments disturb the electrolyte temperature and superheat, which may lead to electrolyte freeze-out or yield loss. Existing ASL demand response methods often rely on oversimplified dynamic models of the electrolytic cell's thermal behavior, such as linear models and the Equivalent Thermal Parameter (ETP) model, which may either violate temperature constraints or underestimate the available flexibility. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a Thermal-Mass Coupled (TMC) dynamic model. The model captures the essential physical mechanisms of electrolytic cells, including alumina feed dynamics, ledge phase-change dynamics, and state-dependent current efficiency. The resulting nonlinear relations are reformulated into a tractable mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model using Taylor approximations and McCormick-envelope reformulations. In the illustrative PBDR and IBDR case studies, the nonlinear reference-model assessment shows that the TMC model achieves net economic improvements 122.4% and 325.1% higher, respectively, than the ETP model. The proposed framework can therefore support deeper demand response participation by aluminum smelters while explicitly assessing adherence to operational safety constraints.

title: Priors and parameterizations for Bayesian regression with categorical variables and interactions
summary: Regression analysis commonly features categorical variables and their interactions to model heterogeneous, group-specific effects. Such interactions are notorious for weak signals and cumbersome parameterizations, and thus urgently require shrinkage. However, the overwhelming default for linear models--using dummy coding, removing a reference group, and applying shrinkage--leads to unwelcome biases, asymmetries, and parameter incongruities across models. We resolve these limitations with a new parameterization-prior combination that couples abundance-based constraints for identifiability with customized shrinkage priors for categorical effects and interactions (BayesABCs). BayesABCs offers a surprising and unique invariance property: the joint posterior of all main effects is (nearly) unchanged by the addition of categorical interactions. We show how this, in conjunction with our shrinkage priors, effectively removes the principal drawbacks of including categorical interactions, thereby making heterogeneous effect estimation broadly feasible. We enforce the identifiability constraints via conditioning and provide a model representation that facilitates efficient posterior computing and direct analysis. Across simulations with a variety of categorical effects and interactions, BayesABCs consistently produces more accurate estimates and predictions, sharper inferences, and unmatched robustness to extraneous interactions relative to competing parameterizations and priors. We apply BayesABCs to study disparities in the error rates of automatic speech recognition systems.

title: Task-Utility IQA: Rethinking Image Quality Assessment in Embodied Tasks
summary: Image quality assessment (IQA) underpins embodied imaging pipelines by judging whether visual quality satisfies downstream tasks, yet most existing methods learn task-agnostic scores aligned with generic human ratings on static benchmarks. This objective mismatches embodied and interactive settings, where image adequacy depends on task goals, context, and action requirements that shape an agent's decisions. We argue that IQA should shift from score regression to goal-conditioned judgment defined by embodied task utility. To this end, we propose an MLLM-based embodied IQA agent framework that reasons about task requirements, grounds quality evidence, and produces decision-facing assessments. A compact VisDrone evidence study shows that conventional perceptual metrics and generic MLLM-based IQA scores are weak proxies for downstream VLM task success, while a task-conditioned utility score better predicts whether visual input supports the target task. These findings support a task-utility-oriented reframing of IQA for embodied, explainable, and decision-aware visual perception.

title: Structured Wavenumber-Domain Channel Estimation for LoS XL-MIMO
comment: Presented at Asilomar Conference on Signals, Systems, and Computers 2026
summary: Near-field line-of-sight (LoS) channels in extremely large-scale multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems exhibit distinctive structural properties in the wavenumber domain. In this paper, we develop a structured wavenumber-domain channel estimation framework that first obtains an initial channel estimate using classical estimators and then refines it through a windowing-based refinement step that suppresses out-of-band noise by exploiting the localized spatial-frequency power distribution. The resulting estimate is subsequently enhanced through a convex constrained formulation that exploits the sparsity and low-rank structure of the wavenumber-domain channel. The corresponding sparsity and rank constraint bounds are selected using a conservative worst-case characterization over the relative position of the transmitter and receiver. Numerical results show that the proposed framework improves estimation accuracy, particularly at low signal-to-noise ratio, by effectively leveraging the structural properties of the wavenumber-domain channel.

title: Anchored Stein Variational Gradient Descent Algorithm for Non-smooth Sampling
summary:
We introduce a Stein variational framework for sampling from a target density $p\propto e^{-U}$ when the target potential $U$ is possibly non-smooth. The key idea is to introduce a smoother reference potential $U_0$ and the anchor weight $a=e^{U-U_0}$. The resulting anchored Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) algorithm is able to target $p\propto e^{-U}$ without computing the gradient of $U$ and include standard SVGD as a special case.
  In particular, we allow the target potential $U$ to be locally Lipschitz while the reference potential $U_0$ is continuously differentiable, along with other suitable assumptions. Under this low regularity regime, we establish a Kullback-Leibler first variation formula for anchored perturbations, identify the corresponding steepest descent direction in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space and prove a nonasymptotic convergence bound for the anchored SVGD algorithm in terms of an anchored kernelized Stein discrepancy. Finally, we also provide guidance on constructing a suitable reference potential $U_0$ based on $U$.

title: Beyond Structural Unification: A Perspective and Roadmap on Unified Multimodal Models
comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Linguistic Principles for Foundation Models
summary: Unified Multimodal Models (UMMs) emerge as a promising way to combine understanding and generation within a single architecture. We argue that current approaches mainly achieve structural unification, which can create a Unification Paradox: shared interfaces, token spaces, and parameters do not guarantee an overall capability gain and may degrade individual capabilities. In this position paper, we identify five critical layers in which unification must be rethought: (1) Asymmetric Input Unification, where models must estimate the utility and reliability of each modality rather than treating all modalities equally; (2) Factorized Representation Unification, where semantic abstraction and fine-grained reconstruction should use separate but coordinated capacity; (3) Stateful Reasoning Unification, where models should maintain and revise a shared multimodal belief state across understanding and generation; (4) Synergistic Optimization Unification, where conflicting understanding and generation objectives require coordinated optimization; and (5) Multi-Centric Systemic Evaluation, where benchmarks must evaluate systemic competence, capability preservation, and cross-task robustness rather than isolated outcomes. We argue that progress requires moving beyond structural unification toward functional unification across the full system.

title: Soft Temporal Alignment Distillation for Camera-to-mmWave Radar Human Activity Recognition
summary: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar provides privacy?preserving human activity recognition (HAR), but sparse point clouds limit its representation of body structure and motion. We propose a cross-modal knowledge distillation framework in which a teacher trained on camera-derived two-dimensional (2D) human keypoints supervises a radar-only student. The stu?dent combines PointNet-based point-set encoding, bidirectional temporal modeling, segment-level aggregation, and lightweight shared latent-channel scaling. The teacher retains contextualized states at every time step, whereas the student summarizes the radar sequence into a small number of segments, making fixed timestamp correspondence unsuitable for feature transfer. Soft Temporal Alignment Distillation lets each student segment adaptively retrieve and aggregate teacher temporal evidence into its distillation target. Alignment denotes student-conditioned representation-space matching rather than chronological or monotonic registration. On the Multi-Modal Non-Intrusive 4D Human Dataset (MM-Fi), the method improves radar-only ac?curacy from 87.04% to 89.17%, achieving the highest mean accuracy among the evaluated established and recent distillation baselines. It also obtains higher mean accuracy and macro?averaged F1 score (macro-F1) than the radar student under most evaluated point- and frame-dropout settings. Adaptation to our independently collected millimeter-wave Office Human Ac?tivity Recognition Dataset (mmO-HAR) improves accuracy from 80.33% to 87.75%, supporting the transferability of the distilled radar representation. The teacher and alignment branch are removed after training, enabling privacy-preserving radar-only inference without additional sensing or computational branches.

title: Causal DAG-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Physical Activity Maintenance: Using Prior Data to Inform Future Deployment
summary: Digital health interventions can provide scalable, personalized support for physical activity (PA), yet sustaining PA over the long-term remains difficult. Because affective experiences with PA are important for activity sustainment, we developed an online reinforcement learning (RL) system for the forthcoming ADAPT factorial trial that personalizes twice-daily activity suggestions aimed at improving affective associations with PA. This setting poses several challenges: participant-specific data are scarce relative to the candidate state space, important states and rewards are partially observed, interventions are frequent while the primary outcome is measured weekly, and activity suggestions can both improve PA-related experiences and increase intervention burden. We address these challenges using an expert-specified causal directed acyclic graph as an integrated RL design tool, guiding state construction, estimation of partially observed states, delayed credit assignment, and representation of beneficial and adverse intervention pathways. We further construct a longitudinal simulator calibrated from a prior micro-randomized trial to compare candidate RL designs under realistic state evolution, missingness, and participant heterogeneity before deployment. Together, this work illustrates how causal domain knowledge and prior trial data can make long-horizon, participant-specific RL more practical for digital health interventions targeting sustained behavior change.

title: People's Views on Smiley Emoji on WeChat Platform, Positive Emotion and Sarcasm
summary: Emoji can easily lead to misunderstanding. On WeChat, [Smile] is often used by the elderly to express positive emotions such as joy and praise, but young people often regard [Smile] as sarcasm. In this case, misunderstandings can easily occur. In order to confirm the existence of this phenomenon and analyze people's understanding of emoji, this study selected 20 smiley emoji on WeChat platform and directly asked people's opinions on these emoji through questionnaires, including whether they recommend others to use, and rating of emotion joy, praise, sarcasm. Analyses were performed based on the total sample and by age group. The results showed that [Smile] and [Bye] were interpreted in opposite ways by older people and younger people. Older people thought they represented positive emotion (joy, praise), while younger people thought they represented sarcasm. Such emojis are easy to misunderstand. On the other hand, some emojis like [Yeah!], both the old and the young have a similar understanding that it represents a positive emotion.

title: Image Modeling: From Handcrafted Priors to Foundation Image Models
summary: This paper unifies six decades of image modeling, evolving from handcrafted mathematical tractable priors to solve inverse problems in imaging to data-driven deep foundation image models for both image generation and solving inverse problems, under a common Bayesian framework that formulates image modeling as an implicit or explicit probabilistic characterization of a data manifold. Every image restoration or generative task fundamentally seeks to answer the same question: What makes an image look like a real image? In the Bayesian framework, this question is encapsulated by the prior probability density p(x), or its more optimization-friendly counterpart, the log-prior log p(x). While early works in solving inverse problems, such as Tikhonov, Total Variation (TV), and Non-local priors relied on explicit handcrafted definitions of log prior to model local smoothness, modern techniques, such as Plug-and-Play (PnP) priors and Denoising Diffusion models, are rooted in algorithmic uncoupling and implicit manifold learning that apply to both inverse problems and conditional image generation. By grounding imaging inverse problems and conditional image generation under a single mathematical engine: the gradient of the log-prior, or the Stein Score Function, we bridge the gap between signal processing and machine learning communities, turning what seems like parallel developments into a single, evolution of image modeling from handcrafted analytical models to models learned from big data, demonstrating that the pursuit of the denoising score is the common thread connecting variational optimization (in MAP estimation) to posterior sampling (in modern foundation image models).

title: Learning on-the-fly quasi-stationarity diagnostics from low-dimensional surrogates
summary:
Accelerated dynamics methods, such as parallel replica dynamics, require estimates of the decorrelation time, after which a process trapped in one of its metastable states is distributed according to the quasi-stationary distribution (QSD).
  In a method proposed by Binder, Lelièvre and Simpson, decorrelation times are defined by coupling a particle approximation of the non-linear conditioned probability flow of the process with MCMC-inspired diagnostics.
  We explore an alternative to MCMC diagnostics, based on coarse-graining of non-linear probability flows and simulation-based inference.
  We first develop a coarse-graining framework for killed Markov jump processes conditioned on survival, proving uniform-in-time, non-asymptotic estimates approximating the non-linear probability flow of
  the true process by the non-linear flow of a surrogate process, defined with a collective variable. The framework does not assume reversibility of the true process, and also gives bounds which scale explicitly in an adiabatic regime.
  Motivated by these results, we then construct a quasi-stationarity diagnostic using simulation-based inference: a recurrent neural network (RNN), trained on particle approximations of non-linear effective flows, estimates posterior probabilities of decorrelation. The learned diagnostic is then transferred to collective-variable traces of high-dimensional particle approximations.
  We investigate the behavior and robustness of this diagnostic on a set of numerical experiments, comparing it to the MCMC diagnostic of Binder et al.\ on both synthetic examples and a molecular system, in and out of its training prior distribution.
  When its prior assumptions hold, the RNN diagnostic outperforms the MCMC diagnostic in ROC analysis, is less conservative, fails less often, and has an interpretable decision threshold.

title: Physiognomy Revisited: How Vision-Language Models Encode Sensitive Attributes Through Image Transformation
summary: Emergent generative AI technologies, while remarkably beneficial across several tasks and domains, can suffer from unforeseen vulnerabilities and difficult-to-anticipate failure modes. Such failure modes can disparately affect vulnerable communities. This paper investigates two well-known vision language models (VLMs) and inspects how these models encode protected identities while generating images. We show that when VLMs are requested to transform human face images to reflect race identities (e.g., Hispanic, Black, White, or Asian) and sexual orientation (e.g., gay or straight), VLMs often comply with such requests. We demonstrate that compliance (and refusal) is non-deterministic, group-sensitive, and generated images are statistically distinguishable, often accentuating deep-seated stereotypes. We further show that representation biases introduced during image generation can re-emerge in textual reasoning and characterization tasks. Finally, we show that this worrisome finding is not limited to racial identity or sexual orientation, image generation can perpetuate bias around criminality, raising concerning possibilities of AI-assisted profiling.

title: Retrofitting centralized air compressor stations with end-use-aware predictive set-pressure control using a physics-constrained pressure-drop model
summary: Compressed air systems usually run at a constant set pressure well above the end-use requirement; the excess margin is wasted energy. A lightweight hierarchical nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) scheme, retrofitted to the sequencing controller of a centralized compressor station typical of small and medium-sized plants, lowers the set pressure as far as the end-use requirement allows. It uses only two pressure gauges (receiver and one critical end-use point) and compressor data, without flow meters or piping surveys. The end-use pressure is predicted by a low-order pressure-drop model identified by least squares under stability, damping and steady-state equilibrium constraints, which serve use rather than accuracy: they let the measured pressure drop be held over the horizon with unit gain. Validated in three stages (plant data, a pipe-network simulator checked against measurements, and the actual controller, at most 1.41 s per update), the NMPC meets the required pressure under real demand and reduces the estimated annual energy consumption by 2.8 % relative to the current constant operation (9.3 % relative to 0.70 MPa). A PID cascade with the same gauge saves about as much only when tuned by a standard rule at its recommended setting from a constant-load step test, difficult in an operating plant; the NMPC needs no such test and keeps its performance with its initial model and default weights after plant expansion and network split. The margin becomes a design parameter instead of a fixed excess, and the controller's signals show where the supply system lacks headroom.

title: Not Just Why, but When and for Whom: Revisiting Common Estimands in Causal Inference
summary: Causal inference commonly defines an individual treatment effect as a quantity that varies across units. But we know such effects, even for a fixed unit, can also vary over time, across repeated studies, or over different methods of measurement, and they can even exhibit inherent stochasticity. In this work, we consider how such additional sources of variation create a need for more general notions of average treatment effects, including some estimands that have yet to be more formally explored by the causal inference community. This perspective also motivates a reconceptualization of our most common existing estimands, such as conditional average, sample average, and individual treatment effects (CATEs, SATEs, and ITEs), as subject to more axes of variation than are typically considered. We explore two main consequences of this reframing in the case where we have data from a single randomized controlled trial: (1) decision making in fixed samples and (2) uncertainty quantification during estimation. We find that different estimands, even for the same unit or the same sample, can qualitatively disagree on whether an effect is positive or negative. We demonstrate these issues empirically through a case study with real data and characterize through a simulation study how our assumptions about these sources of variation, even if we cannot observe the variation, can be consequential for estimation and proper coverage performance. Importantly, these phenomena arise even in the simplest of cases, where all structural and parametric assumptions are satisfied. More broadly, this paper aims to provide a preliminary investigation into an underexplored class of assumptions --- assumptions about unobserved non-confounders --- that should be considered when estimating treatment effects.

title: ReCoPII: A Relation-Grounded Framework for Building Contextual PII Masking Datasets
summary: Training contextual masking systems for personally identifiable information (PII) requires examples distinguishing maskable from preservable mentions of one entity type, but privacy restrictions limit access to real data. Author-based augmentation (SPY) labels mentions unrelated to the author as non-PII, presuming a single data subject and overlooking others. We propose ReCoPII (Relation-grounded Contextual PII masking), a framework that builds such data without this premise: it plans ontology-constrained entity relations, writes insertion sentences with placeholders, reconstructs annotations with code, checks the result with a separate LLM, and derives MASK/KEEP labels from entity relations. On Korean documents from six domains, it yields ReCoPII-Ko, a corpus with relation, privacy, and MASK/KEEP annotations, which we validate. Across 300 pairs, four annotators agree with 88.42% of its sampled KEEP labels, against 26.27% for SPY-style augmentation of the same sources. Classifiers trained on it over-mask less than under that reference on a matched test. Contextual masking fine-tuned jointly with a PII detector removes most over-masking of detection alone within a fixed leakage budget; on human-verified entity records, the four detectors meeting it over-mask at most 5.04% with at most 4.18% leakage. The detector is comparable to XLM-R-large on KDPII with about a quarter of its parameters.

title: Whittle Index Policy for Three State Collapsing Bandits
summary:
Partially observable restless multi-armed bandit models have been studied for dynamic resource allocation problems under uncertainty. This paper analyzes three-state restless multi-armed bandits with partial observability. These are called collapsing bandit problems if the state of an arm (bandit) is perfectly observable when it is scheduled for allocation. The state is not observable when the arm is not scheduled. The planner has a budget constraint on the scheduling decisions in each time slot. The planner's goal is to maximize expected cumulative long term discounted reward. We study the Whittle index policy. To analyze index policy, first the $N$-armed collapsing bandit problem is decoupled into $N$ single arm problems, and convexity and monotonicity of the optimal value function in belief vector are derived using monotone likelihood ratio (MLR) ordering on state transition dynamics and monotone reward structure assumption.
  We next show that the optimal policy is of threshold type in belief under sufficiency conditions on the model. These sufficiency conditions depend on Lipschitz bound on the value function in the belief. We further prove the indexability for an arm using Lipschitz bound on subsidy sensitivity with minimal restrictive assumption on the transition probability model and discount factor $β.$ Our results generalize to three state and strengthen existing results on threshold policy and indexability with weaker model assumptions. We provide index computation algorithm and we present comparison of the Whittle-index, myopic policy and round-robin policies in the simulation study.

title: Setting Things Straight: On the Straightness and Non-Straightness of Two-Step Rectified Flow
summary: Rectified flow (RF) is an ODE-based generative modeling framework that has achieved remarkable success in practice over the past few years. By design, RF seeks to produce flows that have a high degree of straightness, in the sense that the resulting ODE trajectories can be obtained with relatively few (ideally, one) sampling steps. However, a rigorous analysis of straightness or near-straightness of RF flows remains missing in the literature. In this paper, we study settings in which the coupling generated by two-step RF is provably straight at the population level. We provide a complete characterization in two popular classes of data distributions: (i) smooth, strongly log-concave densities and (ii) Gaussian mixture models. Our main results yield sharp conditions for the coupling generated by two-step RF to be straight. Non-straight couplings are constructed when these conditions fail, which demonstrate the sharpness of these conditions. Using the theory developed on the straightness of two-step RF, we propose a notion of approximate straightness that measures the straightness of the learned couplings and can be estimated from the data. We describe a procedure for constructing asymptotic confidence intervals for our proposed notion of approximate straightness and propose a data-driven method for selecting the number of reflow rounds in multiple iterations of RF.

title: What Has Actually Been Proved? Auditable Paper-to-Lean Alignment with LeanTrail
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at the 6th Workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI (MATH-AI 2026), NeurIPS 2026
summary: Compiler feedback certifies that Lean accepts a declaration, not that the declaration captures the intended result: a repository can compile while a central theorem is weakened, merely auxiliary, or transitively dependent on sorry. Formalization progress should instead be measured against the source paper, in terms of its paper items: definitions, lemmas, and theorems. LeanTrail implements this view as a post-hoc, tool-agnostic audit: deterministic retrieval proposes candidate counterparts for each paper item in the Lean repository and, when available, the Blueprint; a language model judges statement-level correspondence, only among those candidates; and proof completeness comes from a deterministic transitive dependency audit never exposed to the model. Fusion assigns each item one of five coverage states, from Formalized to Missing, each backed by inspectable evidence. On consensus annotations of 98 items from three Lean projects, with three runs of each of two judge models, LeanTrail assigns the correct coverage state to 91.8% (Gemini 3.8 Flash) and 92.5% (GPT-6 Sol) of items. 96-97 of the 98 states are identical across runs, and GPT-6 Sol never reports a Partial item as Formalized. Uncovered items form a natural task queue for formalization agents, anchored to the specification rather than the compiler.

title: Static Multipath Suppression in Power Delay Profile of Time-Varying Channel at 28 GHz
summary: This paper investigates static multipath suppression in a time-varying radio channel at 28 GHz using wideband measurements conducted in a dynamic road environment. Two temporal differencing filters and three Doppler-domain notch filtering configurations are compared in terms of their effects on power delay profiles (PDPs) and root mean square (RMS) delay spread. The results demonstrate that all investigated methods effectively suppress stationary multipath components, improving the visibility of vehicle-related reflections. However, differences in filter frequency responses influence the relative powers of dynamic multipath components and the resulting RMS delay spread distributions. The findings highlight the importance of static multipath suppression and filter selection in characterizing time-varying propagation channels.

title: Symmetry Breaking Is the Price of Finite Capacity
summary: If rotating a problem never changes its answer, one might expect its best model to be rotation-invariant; we show that this fails, predictably and by an exact amount, when capacity is limited. A symmetry groups a model's directions into blocks of equally strong directions, a symmetric model must use each block whole, and when the budget cuts a block every optimal model breaks the symmetry. For a Gaussian problem with a $k$-unit bilinear predictor, the log-loss price of symmetry is exactly $(U_k-I_k)/(2σ^2)$, the signal of the best $k$ directions minus that of the best whole blocks. Because an attention head compares tokens through a similarity of rank at most its head dimension, whatever computation precedes it, the same price governs heads fitted to a symmetric similarity by squared error, and heads trained this way on three-dimensional directions break symmetry at exactly the predicted head dimensions, with the predicted rotation sensitivity (RMSE 0.004). Under softmax attention, flatter attention restores the predicted symmetric head where tested, while with peaked attention broken heads beat every whole-shell symmetric head at 16 of 20 head dimensions. We give a procedure that separates capacity-driven breaking from other causes.

title: SCOPE: Source Credibility and Outlet Profiling Engine
summary: We present SCOPE, a multi-agent system for profiling news media outlets with respect to bias, factuality, and credibility. Given an outlet URL, SCOPE coordinates specialized agents for article acquisition, content analysis, external evidence search, scoring, and report generation. The system follows an MBFC-style methodology while making intermediate evidence and agent outputs inspectable through a structured demonstration interface. On a benchmark of 200 media outlets, SCOPE outperforms LLM-only, article-only, search-only, and media-background-check baselines on most metrics, achieving the lowest bias and factuality MAE, perfect failed-fact-check detection, and the lowest factual error rate. These results suggest that decomposed, evidence-grounded agent workflows can support more transparent and reliable media profiling. Our code is available at https://github.com/mbaisbay/SCOPE, and a live demonstration at https://scope-demo.streamlit.app/.

title: A Lightweight Dual-Branch Visual Front-End for Efficient Audio-Visual Target Speaker Extraction
summary: Audio-Visual Target Speaker Extraction (AVTSE) uses face-related visual cues to extract a target speaker from a speech mixture. In many AVTSE systems, visual features are obtained from convolutional image encoders, and their computation may become a non-negligible part of the overall system when lightweight separation backbones are used. This work proposes a dual-branch visual front-end that reorganizes visual information according to its spatial characteristics. A compact lip region of interest is used to model local articulation cues through convolutional processing, while facial landmark coordinates are used to represent global geometric motion with a lightweight temporal convolutional network. The two representations are integrated into IIANet and SpatialNet with limited fusion overhead. Experiments on LRS3-2mix under a unified reduced training protocol show that the proposed method achieves a performance-computation trade-off close to the lightweight image-based baseline. Compared with the ResNet18-based visual encoder, it reduces the module-level visual encoding computation by more than 90% across both evaluated separation backbones, with a moderate performance gap. This comparison excludes face detection and landmark estimation and therefore applies to systems where landmark coordinates are already available from preprocessing. Demos are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Lightweight-Visual-Frontend-E46E.

title: Anytime Valid Confidence Bands for Distribution Functions
